utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we begin as usual by taking the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Office of the Prosecutor, Gerard Dobbyn with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the Prosecution ready to proceed with its next witness, unless there are some other matters that would delay. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I announced that I have a preliminary matter which concerns the motion that we received yesterday by the Prosecution concerning the 65 ter amendment, and three -- those are basically three related issues, and I would like Your Honours' indulgence to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Zecevic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will proceed in Serbian, please. [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I said, these are three related matters. We received, yesterday, a new submission of the Prosecution to change the 65 ter list, suggesting the introduction of a new document related to the testimony of Witness ST-128, who is expected to appear tomorrow or even later today. I suppose that the Trial Chamber will ask us to make our position clear about this submission very soon, and I will do it now. And in the same context, I would like to briefly invoke a couple of facts that we encounter daily in this case and that pose a very serious problem for the Defence. The OTP justifies its motion to change the 65 ter list by the fact that the Defence has presented a criminal complaint concerning a crime covered by the indictment and by the evidence of some witnesses in this case. If that crime is indeed covered by the indictment, and it is, and the indictment, among other things, charges that the police authorities had discriminated in cases when the victims were non-Serbs and conducted less than serious investigations, it is then quite logical to expect, and I have believe even necessary, that the OTP investigating the crime in question reviews the relevant documents in order to establish whether the original investigation had been conducted and what its result was. It is inexplicable, and there is absolutely no justification for the fact that the OTP has still not done it since the beginning of investigations in this case or at least since 2005 when the initial indictment was brought. Some say that this is because the Office of the Prosecutor first issues an indictment and then investigates the case, which our case and similar cases seem to indicate. Your Honours, exactly one year ago, since the beginning of this trial, the OTP has modified or added to its 65 ter list exactly 56 witnesses, which amounts to about 50 per cent of the total number of witnesses in the original 65 ter list. Furthermore, the OTP has -- had made over 50 oral and written submissions to modify the 65 ter list regarding documents and tendered almost 500 new documents, which is about 20 per cent of addition compared to the original number. From the 1st of September, 2009, when the batch 78 was disclosed to us as the last in the pre-trial stage, to date practically an identical amount of documents has been disclosed to us as in the entire pre-trial stage, which lasted almost five years. The amount is approximately 500 gigabytes of documents, and we are currently at batch 137. That means that the increase in documents is 100 per cent, and this continues during the trial. I really believe that this practice on this scale of modifying the Prosecution case in trial has not been recorded so far in any of the other cases before this Court. The very volume of this material makes it impossible for the Defence to do its job well or to perform its duty under the statute and under the professional code of conduct for Defence counsel appearing before the ICTY, let alone the detriment to the guaranteed rights of the accused under the statute, primarily the right to a fair trial. Another thing seems to be typical, namely even on top of this unbelievable amount of material that the OTP is disclosing in trial, for some reason they failed to disclose key documents such as in the case of Witness ST-147, when a very important document was disclosed 90 minutes before his testimony. The same applies to the witness who is about to enter the courtroom and the witness after him. Their evidence and their statements in criminal cases heard before courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning the same crime, and are therefore more than relevant, were disclosed to us just before the beginning of their evidence, plus they were incomplete. I will not even begin to describe how much that documentation is influential on the evidence of the witness who testified yesterday and the cross-examination, because from these documents we can see what the other accused say about the same event and to what extent their stories differ considerably on very relevant points. After receiving and analysing these documents, we will probably be forced to ask these witnesses to return for additional examination. The situation is similar with Witness ST-191. A day after the completion of his testimony, a document was disclosed that relates to the meeting where the witness participated, and the document relates his words, whereas we did not have the opportunity to show him the document and elicit his comments. Instead, the OTP introduced it through Witness ST-182, who has knowledge about that meeting from an unknown and indirect source. So we will also have to ask additional examination for Witness ST-191. Such cases slow down the course of this trial, expose the Tribunal to huge additional costs and inconvenience for the witnesses, and this practice must therefore be stopped. In view of the fact, Your Honours, that this situation is becoming -- is assuming alarming proportions, I thought it my duty to bring these facts to the notice of the Trial Chamber because I believe that they already have and will continue to have a great impact on the further costs of this trial. I therefore ask the Trial Chamber most kindly to take the necessary steps to protect the integrity of these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just like to make a couple of comments about some of the points that have been raised by my learned colleague. With -- regarding the addition of documents over time, we seek to add new documents to the 65 ter list when circumstances require it. It's not a plan that's undertaken by the Prosecution to do this on an ongoing basis, but as circumstances require and arise, we seek to do that. And, Your Honours, each application is looked at individually by the Trial Chamber and is ruled upon according to its merits. We can't take that any further. This is another individual application that has been made, Defence have responded, and we would just be seeking that the Trial Chamber Judge it on its merits. With regards to some of the other points that have come up, the -- the large amount of disclosure recently that has been raised by my learned colleague, I can only assume that much of that is in relation to the new witnesses that we were granted leave to add to the witness list recently, the 44 witnesses relating to adjudicated facts. And the disclosure that comes out of those witnesses has to be disclosed according to the Rules. And as Your Honours are well aware, the Defence has strongly been insisting upon its disclosure as soon as possible. And we are simply trying to do what we can that's required under the Rules and that the Defence wants. Now, with regards -- my learned colleague made a comment about the upcoming witnesses and testimony from the state court which has just been disclosed. And what I would point out, Your Honours, is that the Prosecution found out that the witnesses had testified in the state court in those cases at precisely the same moment that the Defence did, and we sought out those transcripts at the requests of the Defence. It was at their request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We needn't hear you on that particular point. We're aware of the history there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: With regards to the present application, Your Honours, I'm not leading that particular witness. The attorney who is handling that case is not in court at the moment, so I don't know all the specific details. But what I do understand is that it is important to note that the proposed exhibit that the Prosecution is seeking to add was sought and obtained as a result of the Defence tendering into evidence part of the BiH case file through ST-125 on April 2010, and it was after receiving this exhibit that the Prosecution then sought and obtained the entire case file. And I believe that's the subject of this most recent application, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, could I just ask, in clarification of your last intervention, why you didn't seek to have this document added to the 65 ter list much earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, that's not a matter that I have knowledge of. What I can perhaps request is that the lawyer who drafted that motion and who is leading the next witness could perhaps come to court at the start of the following session. And if Your Honours have any questions, he would know this matter in much more detail and could respond much more adequately than I could at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This might be a good idea to call the person down. But in any case, Mr. Dobbyn, the thing that worries the Chamber is that this seems to have become a systematic pattern of last-minute motions for addition of documents to the 65 ter list, and I think we've been through this a number of times before. The Chamber has repeatedly requested the Prosecution to seek addition of documents to its 65 ter lists well in advance of the witness's arrival and to come and testify about these documents, not only so as to put the Defence on notice that this is something that they need to take into consideration in their preparation for cross-examination of those witnesses, but also for the Chamber's possibilities of following the evidence in the case and managing the evidence. So it is, to be frank, Mr. Dobbyn, it's intolerable that we keep receiving these requests in the last minute. It puts the Defence and it puts the Chamber in a lot of distress, and I don't know what other measure we can take than to simply reject your motions. But let's hear from your officer and see if he or she can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, we have received an e-mail communication regarding that, and with regards to the timing, what I understand, Your Honours, is that, as we say, the case file was received in April -- sorry. Just give me one minute, Your Honours. Sorry. It was requested in April of this year. When it was received, it was immediately reviewed for its relevance, and then upon analysing it, it was found that the file in its entirety was relevant. So at that point it had to be sent for translation. As soon as this translation was completed, which was on the 25th of August, it was then -- sorry, one second. So, Your Honours, that was just six days before the filing of this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn. The -- are you ready with your witness, Mr. -- Well, obviously we are not going to rule on this immediately, but we expect to do so in the course of today. Are you ready with your witness, Mr. Dobbyn?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Witness ST-195, Nenad Krejic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, could you inform us of the date on which this case file was disclosed to the Defence? Because I suppose that it was all in Serbian, so they could be notified of the documents before translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and Mr. Smith is just checking that at the moment. It was disclosed on the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir -- good afternoon, sir. Sorry. May I -- can I ask you to make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. I need to point out to you that the solemn declaration that you just made does expose you to the penalties for perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Could you please state your full name and date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Nenad Krejic, born on the 2nd November, 1963, in Radici, Knezevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a teacher of national defence, and I currently work in a security organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And a teacher of national defence, was that your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, sir, is this your first testimony before this Tribunal? Have you ever given testimony before tribunals or courts in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm here for the first time, and I testified twice before the BH court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On matters concerning the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, then, let me explain you how -- briefly how the proceedings will unfold here. You've been called a witness by the Prosecution, who is sitting to your right, and the Prosecution has asked for two hours for your examination-in-chief. After that, the counsel for Mr. Stanisic, sitting to your left, and the counsel for Mr. Zupljanin, sitting for your left -- on your left as well, will cross-examine you. After that, there is the possibility of redirect by the OTP, by the Prosecutor, and the Judges can always put questions to you as well. There is one other practical matter. For technical reasons, we need to take a pause every 90 minutes. And our hearings take more or less four hours, from quarter past 2.00 to 7.00 in the evening or from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00 in the morning. If for any reason you need a little break in between, please tell us and we will accommodate you. That's all I have to say. Thank you very much. And I'll give the floor to Mr. Dobbyn of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krejic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to start off by briefly going through some of your background in relation to your position in 1992, and I know in response to His Honour Judge Delvoie's question you said you were a teacher of national defence. Just to clarify that a little, were you appointed head of SJB Skender Vakuf on 7th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So at that time you were, in fact, police chief of that police station. Now, is it also correct that the municipality of Skender Vakuf, the name was changed to Knezevo sometime in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So just to be clear, when we refer to Knezevo or Skender Vakuf, those names do refer to the same municipality, don't they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you tell me which security service centre or CSB SJB Skender Vakuf was subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The security services centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And did you hold your position as chief of SJB Skender Vakuf until September 1st, 1992, when you were then transferred to CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you were transferred, what position did you hold at CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I was a police inspector, and I performed various duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you also an instructor on the police officer training course in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I was not an instructor. I was a platoon commander at the first police training course organised in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And did you remain in CSB Banja Luka for the remainder of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, in 1992, were you a member of the SDS political party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDS Municipal Board in Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can you explain when you became a member and when you stopped being a member, if at all?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I was one of the founders of the SDS in Knezevo, and I was a member of the steering committee and later on of the Municipal Board. At the first multi-party elections, I was elected councilman in the Municipal Assembly of Knezevo. And later on the Assembly sent me to the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. When I was appointed the chief of the public security station in Knezevo, I resigned all those three posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on from your background now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I would ask that we show 65 ter number 10236.13, and this is a map showing the ethnic composition and distribution in Skender Vakuf municipality in 1991, and it's from page 16 of the court binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this will be coming up on the screen in front of you, Mr. Krejic. Now, Mr. Krejic, you'll see that on this map Serbs are denoted by blue, Croats by red, and Muslims by green. And in the table at the top right-hand corner - if we could zoom in on that, please - you'll see that for 1991 this map shows that approximately 70 per cent of the population of Skender Vakuf was Serb, approximately 20 per cent was Croat, and about 5 per cent Muslim. Now, from your knowledge are these figures correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, if we could move down and see the map as a whole, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, you'll see that on the map it shows that the Croat population of Skender Vakuf was basically clustered in the south-west of the municipality, with one Croat pocket to the north-east of Skender Vakuf, the town named Pavlovici. Otherwise, the rest of the municipality was predominantly Serb, and there are no Muslim-majority areas shown. Is this distribution an accurate reflection of the situation in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: This is quite accurate, in fact. There's just one error here. North-east of Knezevo, it's the village of Pavlovici, purportedly with a Croat population. And that's an error because it never existed. All the rest is correct. But in Skender Vakuf, as it was called at the time, there were Muslims and there are none marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So is it correct that the majority of Muslims in the municipality lived in the town of Knezevo or Skender Vakuf itself?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: They all lived in Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I'd just like to briefly clarify this point about the village of Pavlovici. Are you saying that this village never existed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: It's not a town at all. Approximately in this area it's the village of Bastaja, and there's a hamlet which is part of Bastaja called Pavlovici, but only Serbs lived there. Croats never lived there. It must be just a technical mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with that one correction pointed out by the witness, I would seek the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, Your Honours. I basically agree with what Mr. Dobbyn is suggesting, but it came to my attention actually right now, and I'm really sorry that I missed that, that these maps were created by the Republic of Croatia in 1991, and they -- they actually are aimed in showing the -- the Croatian -- the Croatian population movement between 1948 and 1981. So I don't -- I honestly don't think that these kind of documents can be used in a serious trial because at 1991 this was used as a propaganda, as you can imagine, because it's -- it's only well known that each of the sides were producing maps like this and that. So I would kindly invite our friends from the Prosecutor's side to give us some more reliable maps. I mean, maps as such are -- should be geographically okay, and we might use them for the geography, but we cannot use them for the population numbers because I have a really serious doubt about their accuracy. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, save for maps which are confined to showing geographical features, all maps could probably be criticised as being politically biased in some way or other, and it seems to me that the -- save for counsel giving evidence, which at one point I thought you were in danger of doing, the problem, which the OTP probably accepts, is cured, if cured it could be, by the oral testimony they just elicited from the witness. So in other words, the Chamber would have the map. And to the extent that there are any flaws, the Chamber would then have to look at it alongside the explanation given by this witness or any other witness. But returning to the application to return it, Mr. Dobbyn, I thought we had this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, Your Honours. I believe it's -- it hasn't been shown before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it -- it is 65 ter 10236.13? Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1570, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, I'd now like to turn to another topic and ask you some questions about convoys passing through your municipality in 1992. And while you were chief of the SJB in 1992, do you recall any convoys passing through Skender Vakuf or Knezevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Who was being transported in these convoys?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: For the most part, non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many convoys you were aware of passing through your municipality in 1992 while you were there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but a relatively high number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know where these convoys came from?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: They came from the areas covered by the security services centre in Banja Luka for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you know where these convoys were heading to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: They came from the direction of Banja Luka, and they were heading for Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And Travnik, that was Muslim-held territory, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And at the beginning and in the course of the 1990s, there were also Croat forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any convoys passing in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. Page 16, 10, I believe the witness said during the course of 1992. If you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, I'd like to go back to the answer you just gave. Did you say that "... at the beginning and in the course of 1992, there were also Croat forces there," or did you say during -- at the beginning of the 1990s, "in the course of the 1990s"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the question I was asking, were you aware of any convoys passing in the opposite direction carrying Serb civilians from Muslim-held territory through Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The arrival and transfer of Serb civilians in the opposite direction did occur, but they were not in convoys. It was done in a different way. The convoys, well, that was a difficult situation, too, but the Serbs had it much harder, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, with regards to the convoys moving through to Travnik, do you know who guarded or escorted these convoys?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, they were for the most part escorted by the police from whatever public security station covered the area from which the people hailed, from which they were being moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could I now show 65 ter 3132. This is another map. It's in tab 2 of the Prosecution's documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what we're going to be looking at, Mr. Krejic, is another map of the municipality of Skender Vakuf. What I would like is, with the help of the usher, if you could on that map indicate the route that these convoys took when they were passing through Skender Vakuf towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: So they came in from the direction of Banja Luka, they took this it route to Knezevo, and then they took the old road to Travnik. That's the one. That's the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And on that map, could you indicate the location of Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could just put the number 1 beside that, please.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the map at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1571, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, now I'd like to turn to a specific convoy from the 21st of August, 1992. And around that time, the 21st of August or shortly thereafter, did you receive some information that some people from a convoy had been killed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: How did you first hear about this incident?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The date was most probably the 23rd of August, 1992. In the early morning, my duty officer, policeman, notified me that he had received a report from the duty officer at the operations desk of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre to the effect that in the Koricanske Stijene area around 150 people had been killed. Those people had been in a convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, the information you received from your duty officer, did that also include who the perpetrators of these killings were believed to be?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did the information that you received from your duty officer contain anything about the role of the police escorting that convoy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time where the police escorting that convoy came from?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No, but quite soon after that I learned that this had been the last convoy to leave Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did there come a time where you received information about who the perpetrators of this killing was?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recall the full detail that you received from the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: It was a very brief report, a single sentence, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you recall what the content of that sentence was?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already told you a moment ago to the effect that in the area of Koricanske Stijene about 150 people who were on a convoy were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you find out the specific date, either during this communication or any subsequent time, that these killings took place?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: When I went to the scene, I learnt when the incident had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what did you learn about when the incident had happened?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I learnt that it happened on the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: After getting this call from your duty officer, do you recall if you then contacted anyone yourself?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I contacted the chief of the security services centre in Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what did you tell Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I told him that I had received information, the information that I've just shared with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What instructions, if any, did you receive from Mr. Zupljanin in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me verbatim that I should take the chief of the crime police with me -- or, rather, instruct him to go to the scene immediately. I was to check what was going on and report to him forthwith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you follow Mr. Zupljanin's instructions and go to the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is some error in the transcript. Can the witness repeat the last answer on the line 19, 20 -- 25. Page 19, line 95 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 19, which lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Page 19, line 95 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I have differing numbering here on mine, so is this the question: "What instructions, if any, did you receive from Mr. Zupljanin ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask that question again, Mr. Krejic. When you called Mr. Zupljanin, what instructions, if any, did you receive from him?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was an order to take the chief of the crime service with me, that we go to the scene together to check the initial report, to gather as much additional information as possible, and to inform him as soon as we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You've already said, following that, that you did, in fact, go to the crime scene. Did you take someone else with you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milorad Veleusic came with me, and he was the chief of the criminal investigation service, but he was also, at that time, acting commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the crime scene at Koricanske Stijene, could you see whether or not the location had been secured?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No, it was not secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what did you see when you got to the location?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, at first we didn't know the exact place where it happened. Milorad was driving, and I was looking through the open window at the side of the road. And just on the right-hand side of the road, at the beginning of a very deep canyon, behind some shrubs I noticed down the cliff about a dozen human bodies. That was the first thing I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you subsequently see some more bodies?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: We got out of the car at that spot where I had seen those dozen bodies or so. We looked around and we looked in front of us, and some 30 or 50 metres in front of us it turned out that there were many more bodies. And then we got back into the car, drove to that spot, got out of the car again, and we saw, in our rough estimate, between 150 and 200 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like you now to have a look at a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we could show 65 ter 2266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And while we wait for the photograph to come up, Mr. Witness, did you also notice if there were any ammunition shells on the road where you parked the car or in -- in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we couldn't see anything like that. But even if there had been any ammunition shells, that was not our priority at the time. We were looking at the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, the photograph that's in front of you, do you recognise this location as Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be 100 per cent sure, but I believe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could you take the pen again and mark where you believe the location is that you saw the first grouping of about a dozen bodies. If you could put an X there.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And next to that could you put the number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, could you then mark where you believe you saw the remainder, the 150 to 200 bodies, again with an X. Or perhaps with a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, could we suggest that this is done with the red pen? I think it would be better seen in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could you then draw perhaps a circle around the area where you saw the 150 to 200 bodies.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just a number 2 next to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd seek to tender this photograph now, Your Honours, with its markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1572, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, are we taking the break at the usual time? I'd be happy to do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If this is convenient, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It is a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the Court Usher please switch off his microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I just wanted to add for the record that we have been joined by Ms. Pidwell on the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- you indicated you're joined by Ms. Pidwell. Is she going to respond to the query which the Chamber had on this file as to when it was that the -- in terms of the sequence of events which we have been alerted to when the -- when precisely the Defence would have been -- it would have been disclosed to the Defence and when the Prosecution received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. And I'm sorry, I didn't realise that that had been left unclear. Again, I don't have those full details. The lawyer who is handling that witness does have those details. It was my understanding it's included in the Prosecution's motion. But if not, again, he can come in at the start of the next session. I believe it's in the motion and the information I provided before. I didn't realise there had been any uncertainty left there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry I misunderstood you, because I thought that is what Ms. Pidwell was here to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, for the Chamber to address the objection raised by the Defence, the Chamber would wish to know exactly when the Prosecution received the case file in question. You told us this morning [sic] that you had submitted it to the Defence on 17th of August, yet the challenge was raised in April. So I assume that somewhere between April and August you actually received the file, unless you had already taken possession of it prior to -- to April, I don't know. But the Chamber would wish to have this piece of information as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're looking for that information now. And as soon as it becomes available, I'll let the Trial Chamber know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we have the witness back on the stand, please. Mr. Zecevic, the -- on the application related to 197, we would wish -- we're requesting an expedited response from the Defence by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the request which I have just addressed to Mr. Zecevic, out of an abundance of caution, I say the same thing to you, although I'm not sure that it immediately affects your client. But if you do have an interest in this matter, we would expect your response by tomorrow. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once the Prosecution has given us an explanation as to why this motion had to be filed just a few days ago and not earlier, I would kindly ask you to grant me some time to respond to the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When you say "some time," are you saying that you could not be ready by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would -- well, the way I understand the Prosecution, I would like the Prosecution to explain why once the Manjaca file from the Prosecution was received we received notice on the 17th of August. It was disclosed then. So why did they wait from the 17th of August until the 26th for the disclosure? I would like to get an explanation for that. I have a very important reason why I'm asking for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that's back on the matter of the file that -- yes. Thank you. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, when we left off, you had just described arriving at the scene of Koricanske Stijene and seeing the various bodies in that area. Now, at this time, around the 22nd, 23rd of August, did you have a police unit that was stationed in the Koricani area?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: My police unit was not stationed at Koricanske Stijene but some 4 to 5 kilometres away from it in the direction of Travnik, above the Ugar River canyon to be more specific. And at that time it was part of the Republika Srpska army. It had been reattached, resubordinated, to the Republika Srpska army and was taking part in combat. It did not perform regular police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, this unit, where it was stationed, was this along the route that convoys travelling through your municipality on their way to Travnik would take?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was stationed by this route, and its task was precisely to protect this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: After viewing the crime site, did you go and speak to members of this unit to gather more information?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This convoy had to pass by my unit twice because of the situation, how it was, and I assumed that the personnel in that unit might have some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, in fact, did some members of that unit speak to -- to police who had been escorting that particular convoy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in the unit, it turned out that the police from Prijedor did stop by at the command post of my unit on their way back. They took a short break there. And on that occasion they spoke with the personnel from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you refer to the police from Prijedor, just to be clear, are these the police who are escorting that convoy on the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the statements elicited from the personnel from my unit, it was clear that they were able to identify those people as members of the public security station in Prijedor who had been escorting the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what -- you said that the police from Prijedor stopped -- stopped and spoke with the personnel from your unit. Did you get any information as to what they had told the members of your unit about what had happened to the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The gist of the conversation was this: They admitted that they had killed those people at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did they show members of your unit any property that had belonged to people who were on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, based on what one of the members of my police unit said, the men from Prijedor allegedly showed them money and golden items. But because I know this police officer of mine well, I think it's 50/50 whether it's really true are or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you say it's 50/50 as to whether this is really true, are you talking about whether they had been shown money and gold items?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had doubts about the veracity of his account that money and gold had been shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. After visiting the crime site and speaking to the members of this unit of yours, did you report back to Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately upon my return, I reported to Chief Zupljanin. I told him about everything I had learnt at the scene and also from the personnel from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did that include telling him that the perpetrators were police from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I told him that I had heard from the personnel from my unit, from my police unit, that the perpetrators were from the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And did you also pass on to Mr. Zupljanin the number of bodies you had seen at the crime site?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I did not even attempt to establish the number of bodies because it was impossible to do that from where I stood, but my estimate and the estimate of my escort was anywhere between 150 and 200 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Zupljanin that that was your estimate as to how many bodies were down there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, what was Mr. Zupljanin's response to this information that he received from you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: He said that early in the morning I should come to the security services centre headquarters in Banja Luka, together with two highest ranking people in the Knezevo municipality, the president of the Assembly, Municipal Assembly, and the President of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And who was the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly was Milan Komljenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And who was the president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Vladimir Glamocic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, just to go back, when you reported to Mr. Zupljanin about what you had found at the crime scene, how did you report to him? Was it in person or by -- by phone or some other means?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it was by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, did you go to meet with Mr. Zupljanin as requested with Mr. Komljenovic and Mr. Glamocic the following day?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I considered all demands made by Chief Zupljanin as orders, and I obeyed my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you got to Banja Luka, did you have an opportunity to speak with Mr. Zupljanin privately?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the meeting itself, maybe some five minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what did you tell Mr. Zupljanin when you spoke with him before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I shared with him everything that I had learnt in the field, and I also told him what the position was taken by the key people in the Knezevo municipality, the people in the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what position was taken by the key people in the Knezevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The key people in the leadership, and, in fact, the whole population - the members of the police force, of the army in the municipality of Knezevo - condemned vigorously that act, and they were appalled by what had happened, particularly because in our municipality there had been no war crimes, no mass or multiple murders, and the public saw this incident as something that is going to besmirch our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, after speaking to Mr. Zupljanin privately, you said you attended a meeting. Could you tell us who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Chief Stojan Zupljanin, who chaired the meeting, chief of the public security department in the security services centre in Banja Luka; Djuro Bulic; myself; the president of the Knezevo Municipal Assembly; the president of the Executive Board of the Knezevo Municipal Assembly; the president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly; the chief of the public security station in Prijedor, Simo Drljaca; and I think that there was another person from Prijedor, but I'm not sure about that. I think it may have been the president of the Executive Board of the Prijedor municipality. He is, in fact, the only person I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, was that Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was discussed at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't really look like your normal meeting because right at the very beginning there was a quarrel between on one side the Knezevo people, the president of the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Board, and on the other side the leadership from Prijedor. And at one point or several times, in fact, it almost came to blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: At this meeting was there any open acknowledgement that these killings at Koricanske Stijene had been committed by policemen from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did -- sorry. Were you going to say something further then?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was quite uncontroversial, and the people from Prijedor admitted that it had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You say they admitted that it had been done. What was their attitude towards what had been done? Were they opposed to it? Were they in favour of it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: They thought it was normal, and Simo Drljaca was the most vocal about it, bragging, in a way, of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was Mr. Zupljanin's response to this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: When I met with Chief Zupljanin in private at -- in the morning before the meeting, I noticed that he appeared to be shaken. He was visibly shaken. He condemned the incident strenuously. He called a spade a spade. He said it was a crime. And he took more or less the same position as we from Knezevo did. And Chief Bulic was closer to the people from Prijedor in his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was the conclusion or how did this -- this meeting end? What conclusions were reached as to what should happen next?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: After a lot of quarreling and bickering, Chief Zupljanin insisted on recovering the bodies of the victims. He insisted that those bodies should be identified and, finally, buried. At one point he reacted very harshly to what Simo Drljaca was saying. He told him in no uncertain terms that he would insist on prosecuting the perpetrators of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, did Mr. Zupljanin at that meeting give any specific orders as to any investigatory steps that should be taken, as opposed to steps to remove the bodies from the location?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he could not issue orders to the presidents of the Municipal Assemblies and the presidents of the Executive Boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was he --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry. Was he in a position to issue orders to you, to Djuro Bulic, and Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, was there a point during the meeting where Mr. Zupljanin read a dispatch or letter to those who were present?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you remember the content of that dispatch or letter?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: That dispatch was allegedly sent by the President of Republika Srpska, Mr. Karadzic. He was purportedly at a peace conference abroad. As for the contents, the president from the plains and the president from the mountain should assist the chief of the security services centre to deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was meant or who was meant by the president from the plain and the president from the mountain?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The plain was probably a reference to Prijedor; and the mountain, given our altitude, is -- it was Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Zupljanin insisted that the bodies be removed. Who was put in charge of removing the bodies?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if "removing" is the most fortunate choice of term in this case. If any case, it was meant that these bodies should be extracted from there and buried in a dignified manner, because if we use the word "remove," that could have a negative connotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the poor choice of words, but could you tell us who was to be responsible for recovering the bodies.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: This task befell the municipality of Prijedor. This municipality was more developed. They also had the necessary machinery that was used in their municipality in various mines, and they were tasked with the recovery, the transport, and the burial of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did the fact that police from Prijedor had allegedly committed the crimes have anything to do with those from Prijedor being given responsibility for the clear-up?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That is what the presidents from Knezevo insisted upon. It was their position and their conclusion that if you were up to commit such a horrendous crime, then at least do what you can to recover these bodies and bury them in a dignified manner, exculpating at least a part of your guilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was Simo Drljaca given any specific role in relation to this task?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was supposed to co-ordinate in Prijedor between the municipal authorities and the enterprises that owned such machinery, and also to provide the personnel for recovering the bodies and burying them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: As far as -- as far as you're aware, did Mr. Drljaca ever take care of this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: None of these things were done in the seven or eight days that followed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: If the witness had been told to speak slowly for the benefit of the interpreters, we really don't need him to speak this slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, I've received a message from the interpreters that you can actually speed up in your speech. You don't need to talk as slow. The interpreters will be able to keep up with you. If you just talk naturally. Thank you. Now, sometime after this first meeting in Banja Luka, did you actually meet a survivor of the killings?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of you meeting this person?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The members of the 22nd Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska brought into the public security station of Knezevo one person whom they thought to be a survivor of the massacre at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: How long after the incident was this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When this man was brought to you, did you contact Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I contacted him and informed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What instructions, if any, did Mr. Zupljanin give to you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He ordered me again, very strictly, that I am personally responsible for the security and safety of that person and that I should bring him as soon as possible to the security services centre in Banja Luka and turn him over to the service in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you do as instructed and deliver this man to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately the next morning, as soon as he was brought into my station, sometime around 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you discuss -- once you arrived at Banja Luka, did you discuss with Mr. Zupljanin what would be done with this man?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he told me that he would be turned over to the Swiss Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, did you later attend a second meeting in Banja Luka CSB to discuss the issue of the killings?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you recall the date of the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who attended this particular meeting? Actually, sorry, before you answer that question, I would ask you, Do you recall who called this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly who gave me that information about the meeting. And as for who attended, all those from that first meeting were in attendance, except Chief Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was this meeting again held at Banja Luka CSB?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, you've said Mr. Zupljanin didn't attend, but everyone else from the first meeting did attend. Were there also some other people attending the second meeting who had not been at the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting was chaired by Minister of Defence Bogdan Subotic; and there was also the commander of the 22nd Brigade, Bosko Peulic; and if I remember well, there was also the investigating judge and the prosecutor; then Brane Buhavac, who is chief of the scene-of-crime officers; and two inspectors, one from the police section, that means uniformed police, Dusan Kos, and the other one from the crime investigation police. The last name is Markovic, and his nickname was Muric. And there was also my deputy, my successor, in fact, because I had already received a letter of new appointment transferring me, beginning with September, to the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Brane Buhavac was in attendance and he was the chief of crime-scene officers. Did he inform the meeting as to whether an on-site investigation had yet been conducted between the first and second meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No. He did not brief the meeting on that subject because we all knew that it hadn't been done. Instead, he made a proposal how to go about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was the -- the topic of conversation at this second meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The topic was the recovery of the remains of these people, identification, after which the forensic pathologists would do their job, followed by transport to the place where they would be buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You mentioned that at the first meeting there'd been a lot of tension, arguments between the people from Knezevo and those from Prijedor. Was the tone at the second meeting similar or was it different?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The tone was completely different, either because the meeting was chaired by the minister of defence, member of the cabinet of Republika Srpska, or because as time passed there were more and more people condemning the event, and those who thought it was a normal thing, a matter of course, were fewer and fewer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You mentioned that the topic of this meeting was, again, the recovery of the remains and identification. Can you recall if there were any conclusions reached or orders given at the second meeting concerning investigation of the killings?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Since the hardest part of the work, in view of the layout of the terrain, was to recover the bodies, most of the discussion and conclusions focused on that issue, how to get them out. And then Mr. Subotic, that is to say the minister, mentioned that after that or in parallel with that the security services centre and the competent judicial and prosecutorial authorities would normally conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, apart from removing the bodies, were there any specific steps that were decided with regards to identifying or arresting the perpetrators or otherwise investigating the crime, any specific steps that were decided at the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I've already said that in the course of their discussion, primarily the contributions by Mr. Subotic, it was implied that there would be prosecution of the perpetrators, that they needed to be found and prosecuted, but it was left to the technical services whose job it was to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: After the meeting, what did you do at that point?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: We went to the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was it everyone that went -- everyone from the second meeting who went to the scene?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zupljanin accompany you to the crime scene on this visit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see him that day. He was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the crime scene - this is the second time you'd been there - did you see anything to indicate that the scene had been secured since your last visit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: It was not secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: On the second visit, were the bodies, down in the gorge, were they as exposed to the elements as they had been on your first visit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I knew before and I could see then that a segment of the civilian protection from Knezevo had been to the scene in the interval between the two meetings and cut down the shrubbery and the underbrush and used it to cover the bodies because the inhabitants of the nearby village Koricani, who were using rainwater to drink, complained that the birds and animals were dragging bits of the bodies and carrying them to rooftops, and they had protested in Knezevo why nothing was being done to deal with it, and that's why the civilian protection covered the bodies, so as to make them inaccessible to animals. And that is why when we came to the scene we were unable to see the bodies or find out any more about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And where did you hear this, that it had been people from Knezevo, civil protection, who had covered the bodies like this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I learned that already when I was back in Knezevo, because these people had also been to the public security station to report these incidents. And apart from that, there was an unbearable stench.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you accompany the people from Knezevo Civil Protection when they performed this task?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: No. No. That was not within the jurisdiction of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, on this -- this site visit after the second meeting, was anything other than ways of recovering the bodies discussed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry. I could have phrased that better. The -- during this visit to the crime scene, what was the topic of discussion once you were there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Well, people talked about how these conclusions made back in the office could be applied in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And these conclusions related to recovery of the bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: The conclusion was crystal clear: All the bodies, down to the last one, must be recovered, identified, and buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at the crime site of securing the crime site for evidentiary purposes, for looking for evidence related to the killings that would help you to identify the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC
utterances.text: Quite possibly. But by the nature of things -- or, rather, specifically, I have stomach trouble, and I was about to move to a new job within two days, and my successor was there, the man who would become the next chief of public security Knezevo. I was standing a bit away from the others. It's quite possible I didn't hear any conversation about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to look, if we could, at Exhibit P1567. This is from tab 7 of the Prosecution's documents. And what we're going to be looking at is the amalgamated Vlasic Mountain case file. And if we could go to page 9 in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, the Chamber just wishes to alert you that you have 15 minutes left of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I would ask, if at all possible, that I could have perhaps an extra 20 minutes. I have simply a couple of videos after this that I would like to show. I just want to make sure we get enough time to do those. They are quite important to this whole issue relating to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because much of what you have covered with this witness, we believe, is already included in the adjudicated facts, so if you have videos to show, I suggest you move on to that right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I will. Before the videos, actually, I'll show one more document, and I'll ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also see that it's time for the break. Shall we take that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Before we rise, Mr. Krgovic, just as a matter of clarification, the -- what we were seeking to remind you of earlier was your response to the motion regarding 197 that was filed today. You've already responded to your -- what you intend to do in respect of 1 -- with 128. So we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We are joined now by Matthew Olmsted, who is available to speak about the issue that has been raised with the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Olmsted starts, I would like to announce for the record that Ms. Batista, Ivana, has joined the Stanisic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. First we should apologise. We did not anticipate that this disclosure issue would be such a big matter, otherwise we would have gone into more details in our motion itself. We didn't anticipate a strong objection from the Defence, given that this proposed exhibit is really more or less a continuation of the case file they've already admitted into evidence. So really it's being tendered for this -- the reason of completeness so that the whole file can be viewed in its entirety. I cannot say for certainty exactly when we received this file; that requires some investigation. But looking at our system, I believe it's been entered in sometime in late May of this year, and usually it's entered within a couple weeks of receiving it. So in a best possible world, it should have been disclosed probably sometime in June of this year. Now, during the summer recess, as I began preparing for the testimony of ST-128, it was at that time that I came to review this particular document, at least the analysis of it, and when I found out that it was relevant to ST-128, I at that stage ran a check to see whether it had been disclosed, and it turned out that it hadn't, and at that stage I asked that it be disclosed as soon as possible. And then I sent it for translation because without a translated copy of it, I can't review it to determine whether it's something we actually want to add to our 65 ter exhibit list. And I received that translation last week, and then, talking with my colleagues, I determined that it was something we do want to add to our 65 ter list, and that's when we filed the motion. I hope that clarifies matters at least a little bit with regard to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. Do I understand you correctly that you do not intend to seek admission into evidence of this case file, that you just wanted to include it in the 65 ter list as part of the total case file in that incident for completeness, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I don't understand, Your Honour, but what we intended to do is add it to our 65 ter list at this stage, then I do have some questions with regard to it with ST-128, and at that stage, after he's answered those questions, to tender it into evidence but as -- really part and parcel of the entire file, which is -- part of it which has been admitted into evidence already. So that the Trial Chamber, when it sits down and evaluates this issue, can have both files there and look at the whole thing. The purpose of tendering it is to put into context the prosecution's -- the office of the prosecutor's side of things, and by that I mean the Banja Luka Basic Prosecutor's Office that was functioning in 1992 and how they were processing this case through their system up until -- well, the date of the case file, I think, ends sometime in 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, in order to avoid misunderstandings in the future, I think you should always anticipate strong objections, not only by the Defence but also by the Trial Chamber, for this kind of late-minute -- last-minute motions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We appreciate that. And this was certainly something that we didn't want to happen. We never want this to happen, and -- but sometimes it does, and we will, of course, be -- do our best to be more diligent with regard to this issue in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when it comes to those documents, and more specifically the documents that the Prosecution has just discussed, I would like to make an observation. This document was submitted to us, disclosed to us, on 16th of August, together with some 16 other batches of thousands of pages, and that's clearly Rule 68 material pertaining to the protected witness we completed examining yesterday. And it is indicative that the Prosecution filed a motion to tender this document yesterday. If I had had this document, I would have used it in my cross-examination, and especially in the latter part when we discussed Manjaca. And I did ask some questions of the witness in the course of my cross-examination yesterday, and it was clear to the Prosecution when it received this document as early as in June that this is Rule 68 material. If you look at my line of questioning yesterday and if you look at this document if you admit it, you will see the correlation. It speaks about the role, the place, the chain of command for Witness ST-023. And this is why I have a problem with this kind of disclosure of this kind of material. And if I had had this material, I would have used it yesterday. I would have tendered it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just address that briefly. Ms. Korner's not here, but it's my understanding from my conversation with her last week is that the Defence was alerted to this particular document and even received representations that it might be used during cross-examination of the last witness. Now, I can't confirm that for a certainty without talking to Ms. Korner. Perhaps Mr. Zecevic can confirm that for us. But I believe they did have it and they were aware of it for purposes of cross-examination of the last witness. I know that doesn't touch on this particular motion because this is with regard to a witness who is going to testify tomorrow or Friday, but I just want to make sure that it's clear that - and I'll have to check on this - that the Defence did have notice of this particular document for the purposes of the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we had a different document. It was an interview of another witness. I don't want to mention his name because he might be a protected witness. We couldn't use this interview and put it to the witness, and we were not allowed to put any materials from other witnesses to this witness. So this material was not disclosed to us as Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I heard you say that you would have tendered it yesterday, but do I have to conclude from that that you're not opposed to the addition of this material to the 65 ter list? Or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are two different matters. This is precisely the reason why I opposed to the tendering of documents in this manner. And as my learned friend Mr. Zecevic has said, the Prosecution is throwing tonnes of documents at us, burying us in material. And we get this kind of material at a very late stage, we don't have enough time to go through it, and this is the final result. I would have used it in my cross-examination if I had had it. Now, the question is whether the Prosecution would have allowed me to tender it to that purpose, and this is why I think that the Prosecution opted -- this might be a coincidence, I don't want to claim it, but they decided to disclose to us in this way after the cross-examination was already completed, and this is why I have this concern and why we wanted to share this concern with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can represent absolutely that that was not the intention of the Prosecutor -- the Prosecution in this matter. And, again, I need to talk to Ms. Korner about this, but I believe that the Defence were aware of this particular document or the statements contained within it for purposes of the last witness's testimony because we were under the impression that they were going to use it for cross-examination and they chose not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we bring this discussion to a close - obviously it isn't something on which we're going to rule today - Mr. Krgovic, unless I missed it, I didn't hear you answer Judge Delvoie's question as to whether you -- I understand that you would have liked to have been in a position to use this yesterday, but what is your position now in terms of the reception of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position at this point is the same as the one presented by Mr. Zecevic. So we fully support his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I continue with my questioning ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
